display.purpose: Playlist and track names at hero scale. One per page, never inside a card or list.

headline.purpose: Secondary page headings. Rare by design — used when a section needs named hierarchy.

title.purpose: Card titles, column headers, UI labels. Default for named interface elements.

body.purpose: Track descriptions, metadata copy, contextual explanations. Max line length 65ch.

label.purpose: Supporting metadata: owner, track count, release year, status messages. Not uppercase.

mono.purpose: Durations, progress percentages, track numbers. tabular-nums always active.

shadows.name: content-md
shadows.purpose: Playlist cover image. Content shadow, not UI shadow.

shadows.name: content-lg
shadows.purpose: Track detail album art. Deepest shadow in the system. Exclusive to cover art.

motion.name: ease-standard
motion.purpose: Default easing for state transitions. Used on buttons, inputs, download status.

motion.name: ease-out-fast
motion.purpose: Snappy feedback: hover fills, focus rings appearing.

motion.name: duration-standard
motion.purpose: Progress bar fill, download button state changes.

narrative.overview:
This is the interface a music obsessive built for themselves: precise, unhurried, and quietly confident. The surface is dark by default when the OS prefers it — because album art reads best against a dark canvas, and because this tool does serious work. The green comes directly from the music it handles. Everything else gets out of the way.

The system rejects decoration by principle. There are no rounded corners on interactive elements, no ambient shadows, no gradient fills, no glassmorphism. Depth is created by tonal layering: the page, the card, the raised surface — three distinct levels, no blurring. When the green appears, it means something: a primary action, a live state, a result. Its sparing use across most of the UI makes it land harder on the download CTA.

This is not a marketing tool. It does not need to sell itself. It needs to be fast, clear, and trustworthy — something a user opens, pastes into, and closes with a ZIP in hand.
keyCharacteristics: Sharp corners everywhere on interactive elements (0px radius on buttons, inputs, cards, progress)
Single font family (Geist) across all hierarchy levels
Green accent used as a brand signature — active states, links, progress fill, primary actions
Album art and cover images receive elevated treatment: rounded corners (0.875rem) and shadow
Thin ring-1 outlines replace box shadows for card elevation
Flat-by-default: no shadows on interactive elements at rest
Both light and dark themes are first-class; neither is an afterthought

rules.name: The One Voice Rule
rules.body: Vinyl Green appears on one thing at a time. Primary CTA, active state, or progress indicator — never two simultaneously. Its scarcity makes every appearance decisive.

rules.name: The Neutral-First Rule
rules.body: The canvas is neutral. Color enters only to carry information. Backgrounds, cards, borders, and typographic elements default to the neutral scale; Vinyl Green enters only when a primary action or live state demands it.

rules.name: The Single Family Rule
rules.body: Geist does all the work. No serif, no display typeface, no secondary sans. Hierarchy is expressed through weight contrast (800 → 500 → 400) and size, not family switching. Three weights is enough.

rules.name: The No-Uppercase-Body Rule
rules.body: Uppercase is prohibited for body copy, descriptions, and anything longer than four words. The playlist header eyebrow is the one permitted instance.

rules.name: The Flat-By-Default Rule
rules.body: Buttons, inputs, and cards are flat at rest. No shadow lifts them. If a component needs to feel elevated, tonal contrast is the tool; shadow is not.

rules.name: The Content Exception
rules.body: Album art is exempt from flat-by-default. It is the only element in the system that uses shadow as a structural device — because artwork depth is expected by users and because it gives the cover image visual separation from the dark canvas.

dos: Use Vinyl Green exclusively on: the primary download CTA, active/selected row indicators, link text on hover, and progress bar fill
Keep all interactive elements (buttons, inputs, cards) at 0px border radius
Give album art rounded-xl and appropriate shadow — it is the only surface that earns visual elevation
Use ring-1 ring-foreground/10 for card outlines in place of border or box-shadow
Use Geist Mono and tabular-nums for all numerical data: durations, progress percentages, track numbers
Keep status messages (download progress, error states) inline and single-line
Verify Ghost Light and Ghost Dark contrast on their respective backgrounds before use
Use text-wrap: balance on h1-h3 headings to prevent orphaned last words
Respect prefers-reduced-motion: all transitions should collapse to instant under the media query
donts: Don't add border-radius to buttons, inputs, or cards — sharp corners are the visual identity
Don't use gradient fills anywhere: on text, buttons, backgrounds, or decorative elements
Don't design anything resembling a sketchy download tool: ad-adjacent layouts, warning banners, cramped fields, security-theater iconography
Don't use SaaS marketing patterns: gradient heroes, social proof counters, 'streamline your workflow' copy
Don't make the UI playful or bubbly — no pastel tones, rounded-everything softness, or bounce animations
Don't let the palette drift into default gray — neutrals must be intentional tonal layering, not lazy framework defaults
Don't use box-shadow on buttons or inputs at rest
Don't place uppercase tracked text on more than one section per view
Don't introduce a second font family
Don't clip album art or cover images with 0px radius — they always get rounded-xl
